name: Nabay dialect of Lowland Murut
confidence_why: Prentice 1971 describes non-phonemic penultimate stress only for the Timugon dialect, and his short outline of Nabay (Keningau Murut) covers just the phoneme inventory and the /r/-/l/ contrast, so no source read states where Nabay puts its stress; Cohen 1999, King and King 1984, Lobel 2013, Baboneau 1922 and Mahali 2024 are all silent on it.

new_statements.quote: [2.2.1, p.14] Stress appears to be non-phonemic in Timugon, as its occurrence is always, with very few exceptions (see 2.3.3.3), predictable from the word- and phrase-structure. ... [2.2.1.1] Strong stress (marked by ') occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word ... [10.0, p.274] The next section gives an account of the phonology, including an inventory of phonemes and a description of any distributional or allophonic features which differ significantly from the Timugon pattern. ... [10.2.1.1, p.279, 'The Nabay dialect (Nabai, Dabai, Keningau Murut)'] The phonemes of Nabay are /p t k ' b d g m n ng s j l r y w i u o a/, that is, the same as in Timugon, with the addition of /r/.
new_statements.citation: Prentice, D.J. 1971. The Murut languages of Sabah. Pacific Linguistics C-18. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (334 pp., text present; letter-spaced scanned but fully legible). All three quoted passages are at the stated locators, verbatim apart from scanned spacing: (1) p.26 = print p.14, sec. 2.2.1 Stress: 'Stress appears to be non-phonemic in Timugon, as its occurrence is always, with very few exceptions (see 2.3.3.3), predictable from the word- and phrase-structure. No minimal pairs have been found..'; 2.2.1.1 'Strong stress (marked by ') occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word (see also 2.3.4.1.2): /mamatoy/ 'will kill', /potoyon/ 'will be killed''; 2.2.1.2 weak stress on the first syllable when separated from the strong stress by two or more syllables (/pamamagambad/ 'came…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Prentice's Lowland Murut (described from the Timugon/Poros dialect) word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable; his outline of the Nabay (Keningau Murut) dialect, which by design records only departures from the Timugon pattern, reports the same phonology plus /r/ and no prosodic difference. The penult reading for keni1249 is therefore an extension from the co-dialect Timugon, not a Nabay-specific sentence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Timugon (2.2.1.2): weak stress on the first syllable of the word when it is separated from the strong stress by two or more syllables (e.g. /pamamagambad/ 'camera'); within a phrase the strong stress of a subordinate word is reduced to weak stress. Nothing stated separately for Nabay.
new_statements.exceptions: Timugon 2.3.3.3.1: a few words, particularly those ending in -aCa', are stressed on the last syllable (kaga' 'very', madada' 'dislike', masaga' 'wish'); stress shifts within vowel clusters (2.3.4.1.2: rising diphthongs carry stress on the second vowel; /-io/, /-ia/ finals may leave stress on the antepenult, e.g. /ginio/, /alia/); minimal-looking pairs like tangkung vs tangkuung differ in vowel quantity, not stress. Lobel 2013 writes Nabaay dakî, damî with final stress + glottal (data only).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule (penult of the word, citation forms in phonemic transcription); phrase-level demotion of strong to weak stress in subordinate words. Statement is for the Poros subdialect of Timugon; applied to Nabay only via Prentice's differential outline.
new_statements.identity_note: keni1249 Keningau Murut = Prentice's 'Nabay dialect (Nabai, Dabai, Keningau Murut)' of his Lowland Murut language (Glottolog node lowl1273, which groups Timugon timu1262 and Keningau keni1249). The quoted stress rule is stated for the Poros subdialect of Timugon Murut (timu1262); it reaches Nabay only through Prentice's explicit 'same as Timugon plus /r/' outline, which records no prosodic differences. Ethnologue's other kxi dialects (Ambual, Dusun Murut) are not covered by any source opened. Cohen's Nabay data come from Maasak, Patikang and Limbawan villages around Keningau town.

sources.quote: [2.2.1, p.14] Stress appears to be non-phonemic in Timugon, as its occurrence is always, with very few exceptions (see 2.3.3.3), predictable from the word- and phrase-structure. ... [2.2.1.1] Strong stress (marked by ') occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word ... [10.0, p.274] The next section gives an account of the phonology, including an inventory of phonemes and a description of any distributional or allophonic features which differ significantly from the Timugon pattern. ... [10.2.1.1, p.279, 'The Nabay dialect (Nabai, Dabai, Keningau Murut)'] The phonemes of Nabay are /p t k ' b d g m n ng s j l r y w i u o a/, that is, the same as in Timugon, with the addition of /r/.
sources.note: Sec. 2.2.1 (p.14, Timugon/Poros dialect of Lowland Murut): stress non-phonemic, predictable; strong stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; weak stress on the first syllable when separated from the strong stress by two or more syllables; a few words (esp. in -aCa') stressed on the last syllable (2.3.3.3.1). Sec. 10.2.1.1 (p.279) Nabay [= Keningau Murut]: phonemes 'the same as in Timugon, with the addition of /r/'; the outline is explicitly limited to features differing from Timugon (10.0, p.274) and lists no prosodic difference -- i.e. no Nabay-specific stress sentence.
